utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-04-75-T, the Prosecutor versus Goran Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. May we have the appearances, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Matthew Olmsted and Thomas Laugel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. For the Defence, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Defence of Goran Hadzic, Zoran Zivanovic and Christopher Gosnell, with Case Manager Negosava Smiljanic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Could the record reflect that we sit 15 bis; Judge Mindua being absent. Mr. Zivanovic, we were told that you have a matter to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Your Honours, the Defence seeks an extension and clarification of Your Honours' decision of 3rd September 2014 so that it may include permission to exchange documents with all Defence witnesses who are detained at the Detention Unit. In Your Honours' decision at paragraph 6(iii), you ordered that "the Registrar to permit the exchange of documentary material between the Hadzic Defence and DGH-045 through DGH-045 legal advisor in anticipation of DGH-045's appearance as a witness in this case." The Defence understood this order to apply mutatis mutandis to all its detained witnesses. Yesterday, a number of issues arose during the proofing the DGH-046 that did not, in the Defence view, comply with that order. The Defence delivered on Friday, in accordance with UNDU regulation, a binder of documents the witness's counsel so that they could be delivered to the witness in order to prepare for this -- for and streamline my upcoming interview. When the proofing session began, the witness was prevented from bringing the binder with him from his cell, although his counsel was present to receive those documents from him during the meeting. As a consequence, the proofing process was obstructed and the review of documents was impeded. Yesterday morning, I brought another binder of new documents which I gave to the witness counsel again, but this time his counsel was not permitted to provide the document to the client. As Your Honours are aware, the Defence will have at least five witnesses who will be proofed in the Detention Unit. We would therefore request that the Trial Chamber affirm that the Defence may surrender the documents to any witness at Detention Unit through his counsel, and we would also seek a modification of Your Honours' order to allow the witness to bring these documents to the next proofing session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, is -- do you have the witness ready?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Before he entered the courtroom, I would just inform the Chamber that we have on our list five documents from our fourth motion to amend our Rule 65 ter list, and I would ask the Chamber to admit these documents under our Rule 65 ter list. These documents are 1D3766, 1D3767, 1D3768, 1D3769, and 1D3770. And we would also like to add four documents to our Rule 65 ter list that we put on the list of exhibits for this particular witness. These are 1D3761, 1D3777, 1D3778, and 1D3779.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It would be helpful, Mr. Zivanovic, if you could provide us with tab numbers from your exhibit list for the --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I suppose we are on the list, right? Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: 1D3761 is 671. 3769 is 672. Sorry, it -- it seems that 1D3761 is actually 3768. It is number -- tab number 671. 1D3769 is 672. And 1D3770, it is 673. 1D3761 is 638. 1D3777, 714. 1D3778 is 715. And 1D3779 is 716. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. Could the witness be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Sorry, I omitted 1D3646.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is tab -- I -- sorry. I omitted 1D3646. It is tab 713.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Is there a position from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just taking a quick look at these exhibits, the Prosecution has no objection to 1D3766, 3767, 3768, 3769, 3770, 3777, 3778, and 3779. All of those documents the Prosecution has put on its own list for this witness and therefore doesn't object to them. With regard to 1D3761 and 1D3646, the Prosecution does object on the grounds of look of due diligence and late notice with regard to those two documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Susa.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I take it you can hear me in a language you understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear you very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you for coming to The Hague to assist the Tribunal. May I ask you to state for the record your name and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Vojin Susa. I was born on the 14th of August, 1957.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Susa, you are about to make the solemn declaration by which witnesses commit themselves to tell the truth. I must point out that by doing so you expose yourself to the penalties of perjury should you give false or untruthful information to the Tribunal. Could I now ask you to read the solemn declaration the court usher will give to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Zivanovic, I'm -- I was wondering whether we should first finish the business with the documents. Two documents are objected to by the -- by the Prosecution. Do you have a reply for that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. As far as I know, 1D3646 was one of associated exhibits from the Rule 92 ter statement that we submitted to -- to -- so as far as I know, it is not new document at all. And for 1D3761 -- 1D3646 is amendment of the -- sorry, 3761 was amendment of the constitution of the RSK, and it is known -- this document is known to the Prosecution for a long time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: All these documents, I don't think I need to repeat the numbers, but all of them are -- can be admitted to the 65 ter list, including the two the OTP objected to. Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Susa.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I want to introduce myself for the record. My name is Zoran Zivanovic, and I appear as Goran Hadzic's counsel in these proceedings. First of all, I would kindly ask you to tell us where you were born and where you lived before 1991.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: As I have said already I was born on the 14th of August, 1957, in Vinkovci as part of the Republic of Croatia which was one of the republics of the SFRY. After birth, shortly afterwards, my parents were employed in a nearby village called Stari Jankovci. I grew up in that village and completed primary education. Then I completed gymnasium high school in Vinkovci and studied law in Osijek. Having graduated from the law school, I became employed as an intern with the public prosecutor's office in the municipality of Vinkovci. Having passed the bar exam, I was appointed to the position of municipal public prosecutor in Vinkovci. I occupied that position until September 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Have you testified before in any proceedings before this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Yes, in 1998, in the case against late Mr. Dokmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In those proceedings, did you provide a written statement to any of the parties?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: In those proceedings, I was heard as a Defence witness by the Defence team headed by Mr. Toma Fila. I also provided a statement to the OTP Prosecutors. As regards the topics discussed with the Prosecutors, a voluminous statement was drafted in English. The interview took place in English as well with the presence of an interpreter. I spoke in Serbian and the interpreter interpreted it into English. The gentleman addressed me in English and it went through the interpreter again. The procedure that was applied was fair, and I signed that statement in English. I signed it in the office of Toma Fila, the attorney-at-law, when the statement was brought in by Mr. Vasic or, rather, his assistant. At that time it had not been translated into Serbian. In my presence, he reviewed it and read it and said it seems to be fine, so I signed the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you also provide a statement to Mr. Dokmanovic's Defence?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Describe for us briefly the interethnic relations in Croatia before 1990.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: In my estimate, there were good interethnic relations. In the village where my parents worked as teachers, I grew up in the part of village inhabited exclusively by Croats and Hungarians. All of my childhood friends, some of who remain to be my friends, are Croats and Hungarians. As for any discussions based on ethnicity, it simply did not exist. The entire society was expanding. In my view, we developed individually as well as collectively, education was free, and most people -- or basically all of them had jobs. We had good social security and the situation was fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did the situation change in the 1990s?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Unfortunately, yes. As I said, I worked in the municipal prosecutor's office. In addition to standard measures of prevention and sanctioning of crimes, the prosecutor's office is also engaged in carrying out assessments in the field in order to follow certain trends in the society that may cause turbulence or shifts. In the late 1980s, starting, say, with 1989 and 1990, and especially in 1991, we observed that when labourers who worked abroad came back, and had it happened in terms of cycles around Christmas, Easter, and summer, the topics they discussed became increasingly political. There was already mention that the way the SFRY was set up became obsolete and that different social relations needed to be established; i.e., that capitalism needed to be introduced. There was mention that the relationships between the socialist community was not set up properly and that the developed republics such as Slovenia and Croatia were being held back as well as that situation needed changing. There was also discussion about too many Serbs being in senior positions in Croatia either in the economy or the political system. It gained additional momentum in late 1990 and early 1991 when, in Croatia, political emigres became resurfacing in Croatia. Starting with the 1970s onwards, they had problems with the law because of their chauvinism and nationalism and the way they expressed their ideas. If I may, I'd like to add something. Those stories were untrue. For example, I gained employment with the public prosecutor's office in the municipality based on the ethnic principle. What does that mean? It means that certain positions in the judiciary, police, the economy, were going to be occupied relative to the ethnic structure in the particular -- in a particular area. The public prosecutor's office in Vinkovci had the prosecutor and four deputies. I was the only Serb out of those people and that place was supposed to be assigned to the Serb community. I occupied the position of Mr. Branko Mijovic who had proceeded me in the prosecutor's office and then went to the investigation centre of the district court in Osijek. That relationship was also reflected in all other segments of society pertaining to ethnic figures.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me briefly in early 1990 what was the position taken by the Serb population in Vinkovci and the surrounding area?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Well, I can only tell you how we experienced it within my family. We're Serbs so this began to cause a certain amount of disquiet. In the beginning, it wasn't fear but it was a kind of disquiet because particularly as far as my parents were concerned the direct memory of World War II was very strong. We later generations experienced that differently but they experienced it personally in their lives. My family, which is not a large family, in the period of 1941, the family, which lived in a number of houses, numbered about 20 of us with the same last name. Four people were between 16 and 25 years of age and they ended their lives in concentration camps from that family, these were my father's brother and sister, and he remembered all of these events as a family tragedy. And, of course, this was something that disturbed the people, made them feel disquiet and among some of them there was even fear.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us how the authorities at the time reacted to these events in Croatia? Did they try to calm things down?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: The authorities at the time were still trying to calm things down. In the period of 1989 and 1990, the state organs viewed on this as something that was not good. But no specific actions were taken in terms of initiating investigations or anything like that. All of that was in a phase of rest. In words, we were in favour of action but we actually never took any action.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us what happened after 1989 and 1990, what happened after that?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: After that -- thank you, yes, it's probably my fault. We were getting ready and we were waiting for multi-party elections. In these preparations for the multi-party elections, many political rallies were held, many parties were being established. Other than the old League of Communists that transformed in Croatia by introducing a series of liberal and free-thinking positions, all the other parties that were founded unfortunately were a bit more nationalist and they vied with each other as to which one would emphasise more the idea that Croatia belonged to Croats and that there should be political and economic independence of Croatia. In some areas of Croatia inhabited by a majority Serb population, parties were founded that were ethnically Serb. I think the worst position was for us, people from urban areas, who at some point did not belong anywhere anymore, neither here nor there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know if there were any specific events that particularly disturbed the Serbian population in the area where you lived?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Well, you know, incidents that boiled down to verbal and then later mild physical altercations began already from 1989 through 1990 and 1991. I myself, at that point in my life, didn't notice any particular changes towards myself. I don't know whether that was because I'm that sort of a man or because of the fact that I was in a respectable post, but nobody exhibited anything bad towards me. Things began to complicate significantly after the HDZ won elections. Everything that went around, talks and threats, actually, began to materialise. It was compulsory in work organisations for you to sign those infamous statements of loyalty to the Croatian state. Even though you did not question in any way the integrity of the Croatian state, nevertheless you had to affirm this in this written document. And the process began in which many Serbs lost their jobs, responsible positions. For example, in my family my wife lost her job, but she actually stayed in Stari Jankovci. She was a music teacher in the elementary school. She lost her job because of her professional qualifications, allegedly, but actually that could not have been questioned because after her they gave the job to a person who was less qualified than she was. So, in conversations with other people, I learned that in their areas as well, perhaps in their families too, the same kind of things were happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that when the HDZ came to power, they introduced some legal measures that had an effect of interethnic relations. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Yes, the constitution was amended so the main body of the constitution, the founding document of a state, Serbs were erased as a constituent element. This represented a serious threat and a danger to the Serbs. I recall -- or I would like to remind that Croatia, the way it was, the Croatia that I was born in, was established after Second World War, after the peoples' liberation fight, and after the pro-Fascist authorities left who formed the so-called independent republic of Croatia from 1941 to 1944. This second Croatia was created on the basis of laws post-World War II and the Serbs paid for that with vast casualties. I wouldn't want to speak about those casualties because I don't want to be accused of bargaining with those casualties, but I must simply say that those casualties were vast. They were not just casualties as a result of direct fighting with the occupation Fascist Nazi forces. The tragic thing is that those casualties were a result of numerous concentration camps such as Jasenovac, Stara Gradiska, Jadovno, and the most awful of them all, the only concentration camp recorded for children, the one in Jastrebarsko. So after all of those casualties, the Croats and Serbs were together in these new organs of power and they established the Socialist Republic of Croatia within the Socialist Federal Peoples' Republic of Yugoslavia which was later renamed to the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia. By being deleted from the constitution, the Serbs got a very ugly message, and also in the press every day you could read very ugly articles about how the Serbs usurped power, they took more than they had a right to, and that this had to come to an end.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Besides being removed from the constitution and reading articles in the paper, can you please tell us if any other things happened that made the Serbs feel threatened? Were there any events that would indicate that there would be an armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Well, these were not events. It was an ongoing thing. Already in early 1990 -- and it became more and more frequent from the mid-1990 onwards, for example, in Vinkovci you could notice armed persons in classic military uniforms. I asked myself for a long time what these units were, who do they belong to. In view of the fact that I had good connections as deputy prosecutor, I had connections in the police, so I was able to ask the people from the police whether those units were under their jurisdiction, and the answer I would get would be, "No. These are some other units. We don't know who is setting up these units." Evidently by the insignia that they wore, they did not belong to the Yugoslav People's Army either, the only regular army that existed at the time in the territory of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia, including Croatia. Later, we learned that those units were called ZNG, National Guards. What's very typical and important is that members of those units could only be Croats which indicated that a special formation was being created, a police or a military one, we didn't know which one at the time, because already at the time because of that approach constituted a threat to the Serbs. At the beginning the units were located in areas which were not areas where any police or military formations were supposed to be, these were training camps, stadiums. Already in late 1990 or mid-1990, these units began to appear in public. They had their patrols. They checked traffic and persons and they did this particularly in areas where there were Serb villages. This caused unpleasant scenes, people were brought out of their cars, they were taken away for interrogations, their vehicles were seized, and there was even physical force applied which in this phase would be restricted to beatings and so on. But in this first stage people were allowed to go home and the most extreme things did not happen yet where people would disappear.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And appearance of these armed formations and generally the arming that was going on at the time, how did that affect the Serbian population in Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Well, it's easy to conclude on the basis of what I have just said that the Serbs were uneasy, and the Serbs began to organise too. They self-organised. People were slowly beginning to form those village guards which during the night would control who was entering the village in order to prevent any incursions. Records were kept of who was interrogated and taken in on a particular day. I think that among the people in the area where I lived, this caused a most serious degree of fear.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And now that we're talking about fear, are you able to tell us what it was that Serbs were afraid of at the time? The army existed, there was the police. So what sort of a fear was it among the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: I must tell you that initially the army, in a way, could not act. It was sidelined. The army as we knew it was not formed in order to prevent internal conflicts within Yugoslavia. This is something that was primarily done by the police. So people knew that only by self-organising could they get any results because people, you know, they would come to the prosecutor's office when I worked there and they would also go to the police, they would report cases when they were mistreated and when without any warrants their vehicles were seized or other valuables. Police -- the police would say that this was not under their jurisdiction. They said that these were not the units that they had sent out into the field. We in the prosecutor's office, we did not get any investigation reports that we could act upon, and judging by what people told me from Mirkovci, a neighbouring village where my cousins live, for them, all of that was a sign that they had to do everything to secure their own protection; the protection of their families too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at 1D1201. This is tab 257.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You had the opportunity probably to see this petition signed -- well, it was sent by the Serbian inhabitants of Stari and Novi Jankovci, the villages that you have talked about. Could you please tell me -- well, they cite a series of details about events that were happening about worsening interethnic relations, about incidents, so what I would like to know is if you had any information about this worsening of interethnic relations in Stari and Novi Jankovci?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: All -- I know all the people involved in these unfortunate incident, both Serbs and Croats. I lived in Stari Jankovci until I was 27 years old with many of these people. I grew up with them. Yes, unfortunately, everything that is stated in the petition is true. I was informed about it directly. When the petition was drafted, the people informed me that they were going to do it. They asked me if there was any point in doing it. I said that, yes, there was some point in addressing the state organs and asking for their protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us, do you know if the organs acted upon the petition?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Unfortunately, no. Nothing was done. It was just recorded as an incident that would be investigated. All the elements of it would be established, but nothing was actually done.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: On the second page of the same document we can see a reference being made to the events that happened on the 5th of May, 1991. I can see that that followed the incident in Borovo Selo. Do you know - and if you do know about that incident in Borovo Selo - what happened?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: That was on the 2nd of May, 1991. I was near Zagreb. I went there with my son to attend a tennis tournament. Something happened on the 2nd of May, and I learned about that on the evening news as I was watching Zagreb television. On the following day, I returned home. I already had the information about all that. I had inspected and perused official documents, and it was obvious that the first incident of very low intensity happened on the 1st of May. It was about flags being hoisted. The 1st of May is the international labour day, and on that day people in Borovo Selo hoisted a Yugoslav flag. Two Croatian police officers came. They took the flag down and replaced it by a Croatian flag. There was a verbal argument as a result of that, and I believe that some of the villagers of Borovo Selo beat one of the police officers. The police officers left, they reported on what had happened, and then on the 2nd of May a police expedition arrived in Borovo Selo. They arrived two buses, there were about 100 armed men on those buses, they were well armed, and this started the notorious conflict. As soon as they got off the buses, the police officers started shooting. The man who was sitting in front of the local commune building was killed. Obviously they had informers in Borovo Selo and they knew that armed policemen had set out against them, so the villagers of Borovo Selo were well-informed. They knew that there were armed policemen coming, they returned fire, and as a result some Croatian police officers were killed and a lot of the villagers of Borovo Selo were wounded. We can see that the incident in Stari Jankovci happened on the 5th of May, after the burial of one of the police officers who had been killed. By way of retaliation and revenge, the incident happened in the way it was described in this petition.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 1D1201 will be Exhibit D214.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you now please tell us in very general terms what was the effect of the incident in Borovo Selo in Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Members of the formation that we have already mentioned, the ZNGs, started getting more and more involved in the happenings. They were fully armed. They had long-barrelled weapons. They started patrolling Serbian villages and blockading them. These were not full blockades, which means that you could go in and go out. However, the controls became very, very rigorous and people were ill-treated on a daily basis. Unfortunately, I have to say that people were also beaten and that was considered to be very normal. The Serbs started withdrawing to their own villages, and when they did leave them, in order to do chores or buy provisions, those ended up in incidents. They were taken to the police stations, they were kept there, they were interrogated. Some extreme happenings were recorded, people went missing, they never returned to their homes, arms were being more often used against people in their fields in the zones of those Serbian villages. A lot of people were wounded and quite a few were killed as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: After these incidents, did people start moving out from Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem or in to the province?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Unfortunately, when it comes to more permanent settlement, very few people settled in Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. During the first phase, people started moving out, albeit it slowly, first from the areas bordering on Croatia. And both peoples moved out from there. People who were Croats moved to Croatia, and people from Serbian villages started moving out to Serbia. The first ones to leave were the women and the children and the infirm. Those who remained were young people who were ready and prepared to defend their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What about your personal experience? What did you experience in the course of 1991 at the time when interethnic relations worsened?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: In 1991 at the very beginning, I believe that that was in the month of February, I was taken to the hospital for a gall-bladder surgery. The surgery was successful. I felt well but I was very ambitious and I thought that I was feeling better than I actually did. That's why I had to stay on sick-leave for longer than intentionally planned. As I was recovering, I was in my house in Vinkovci. I moved about the town, and I walked by a barricade. Every day I had to pass by a barricade which was some 100 metres away from my house in the direction of the town centre, and it faced the village of Mirkovci. That barricade was constantly manned by some 30 or 40 people, some of them in uniform, some of them in civilian clothes, but in any case they were all armed. Those people knew me. Some of them were my neighbours and they did not pose any problems to me. I could move freely around that barricade. Those barricades, both on the Croatian and Serbian sides, is where shots were heard at dusk. Shots were fired from infantry weapons. Mirkovci and Vinkovci actually are not two separate settlements. They are only separated by a railway line and you really don't know where Vinkovci stops and where Mirkovci starts. In Mirkovci some 500 metres away from the barricade that I have mentioned, there was a Serbian barricade. Every night over the roofs of our houses bullets were flying. We didn't feel safe, but we did not have any other option but to remain living in our houses. On the 9th of July, 1991, after what was possibly the strongest fire that forced all of us in the house to spend the night in the basement, several bullets ended up in the roof of our house. I was sitting with my mother and my wife on the terrace of our house. The morning was sunny and warm. We were drinking coffee. My father had gone to fetch bread. Some 30 to 40 members of the ZNG formation burst into my courtyard. They did not have any search warrants. I asked them what that was all about, and they told us just remain sitting. Don't move. Their weapons were aimed at us and they were cocked. They entered the house. My wife was afraid because our older son was in the room sleeping there. He was 12 years old at the time. She told them there's a child asleep in one of the rooms and a guy responded, "We do not shoot children." They chased my son out of the house and they start searching the house. One of the guardsmen were standing next to me with his rifle aiming at me. I asked him what was happening, and he said we have a report that shots were fired from your house onto the barricade that. That was crazy. It would have never occurred to me to provoke anybody from the house where I was living with my closest, my wife and children and my parents. I only had a hunting rifle in the house and they are used -- such rifles are used only in game hunting. And I also had a pistol that I was issued as a member of the prosecutor's office. I believe that it was the red -- the Crvena Zastava pistol, 7.65. Those weapons were locked in a cabinet to keep them away from the children. So I kept the weapon safe in the cabinet. When the search of the house was completed, and while they were searching the house they broke things, they overturned furniture, there was a lot of damage as a result of that search. I asked them, "Who is your superior?" And then a man introduced himself to me and said, "I'm the one. What do you want?" And he introduced himself to me as Cigo and he said -- I said to him, "I am the deputy public prosecutor in Vinkovci. Here's my official ID." He took that ID and tore it apart. I asked him, "How can you do that?" And he said, "You will tell us everything you have to tell us within the next couple of hours." They did not handcuff me. They pushed me into a van and we started driving through the city. We stopped in front of the football pitch of the football club that was called Dinamo at the time, now it is Cibalija, a gate opened. There is a high fence around the football pitch. I knew that because I had attended football games at that stadium many times, many times before. I saw a lot of members of the ZNG in uniforms. I was taken to a bench. There were several benches in the courtyard. Those were metal benches, fixed to the ground. They told me to get out of the van. I did. And then they handcuffed me. They actually handcuffed me to the bench, and I remained sitting there. Nobody ever said anything to me at that point. And then there came a time when a door opened and a large group of people, some 40 or 50 people, entered the cart yard. They were all members of the ZNG. I noticed several wounded among them because they had blood-drenched dressings around their heads or arms or legs. I heard that that unit had attacked people who were doing harvest near the village of Pacetin but that the villagers tried to defend themselves using weapons and they wounded some of the ZNG members. While they were passing by me, one of them or several of them wanted to know who I was. And somebody else said, "He is a Chetnik. He had opened fire on us last night." Some of them started savagely beating me as if they had been given the signal. They beat me on the head, on the body, on the arms. I lost consciousness and I suppose that I fell down by the bench. When I came to I was sitting on that same bench and two lads from the ZNG unit whom I recognised as villagers of Stari Jankovci, one of them was Jurisic and the other was Zecevic, they obviously knew me and they were rinsing my face with the water from a plastic jerrycan. Jurisic told me, "Don't worry, they will not kill you." Obviously I was hurting from the beating. I was sitting. And I realised that I was missing some teeth. And then I -- I -- I realised two or three of my teeth were missing, and I also had a strong pain in the right chest and the right shoulder. My arm was crooked. My right arm was somehow crooked. I told him it seems that my shoulder was broken, and they said no, it's probably just twisted. And then they left. I was sitting there for some 10 or 15 minutes with my head bowed. I was bleeding from my mouth and from my nose. A group of some four or five of them arrived. They uncuffed me. Actually, they cuffed me again and they took me to what they called a face washing. That face washing actually entailed another round of beating in the toilet. One of the guards then pulled a pistol. He put it in my mouth. He pushed it forcefully and then I realised that something was breaking. I -- there was a cracking sound in my jaw. The nickname of that person was Sokac, but it's neither here nor there. I fainted again and they brought me to by pushing my head into the toilet bowl while somebody was flushing the toilet bowl. I heard one of them saying, "You're really going to kill this guy." They dragged me -- or carried me rather than dragged me to that same bench and they tied me to it again. I believe that a couple of minutes passed before a window opened on the first floor and a young officer appeared on the window. He had patches on his shoulders. I don't know what the patches signified. I know that he was sporting spectacles and he said, "You're going to kill this man. Bring him upstairs." Two members of the ZNG came to fetch me. They had not participated in the beating. They literally held me under their arms and they carried me to that guy's office. I found my father there and a friend of ours, Bosko Racanovic. That same morning he had heard the terrible shooting. He knew where our house was and he came to our house to see whether we were all alive. Bosko was bleeding from his nose, my father was -- my -- my -- my father's face was red so I knew that somebody had slapped him around. They were not otherwise injured. On that officers desk there was a military uniform, and when I say "military" I mean a JNA uniform, and there was also a rifle which was not mine. There was also my rifle, my official pistol, and two grenades. At that moment, a door opened behind us. A cameraman arrived and took photos of the entire situation. He left. Nothing happened. That that commander asked me whose weapons are these? I couldn't speak. I was bleeding from the mouth and that blood was pouring all over my body. My father saw that. He started crying from fear when he saw that. I only told him that those were not my weapons. I pointed to all the weapons. And he says I know and -- some -- some of it is yours and the rest belongs to somebody else. He took a grenade, he hooked it to his belt, I saw that there were no other grenades on his belt, and another man who was there took the other grenade, and I realised that those grenades belonged to them. He ordered to his subordinates to take us to the police station. He said, "You're now going to be taken to the police station, they will take your statement, and then everything will be fine." We went to the police station, my father and Basko Racanovic were taken to a room, and they kept me there, exposed to everybody's views, in a hallway behind the public desks. The guards who remained there and kept me at gunpoint asked me to remain standing, although I wanted to sit down. There were people coming to those desks on their business, and they were in a state of shock. They were wondering who I was. And the reply they received was this is a Chetnik who had opened fire on us last night, and this is how everybody of that sort would fair. I wanted to lean against the wall. He pushed me away from the wall and said you are staining the wall with your blood, which is true. And then there was this staircase leading to the first floor. At that moment a member of the ZNG started coming down, that was Cigo whom I already mentioned, and he said to -- to -- tonight you will see what will happen. And that's how I remained standing. Nobody approached us. None of the citizens. None of the police inspectors. At that moment my uncle came from the city. He probably heard that we were there and in his car he transported us to our own house. At home my wife and my mother were trying to put order into the house. I saw them crying. I saw them afraid. And a friend of mine, a Croat, came and told me, "Vojo, I'm begging you, go somewhere. Don't stay. Don't wait for the night-fall in the house. I am afraid that something bad will happen to you. I can't help you and I will feel terrible if something bad happens to you." I had already made my decision. A friend of mine came, another Croat from Vinkovci, a doctor. He tended to my wounds as much as he could and he told me that -- my jaw looked the worst. My pallet looked the worst. He tried to use tampons to close the wound on my pallet. He succeeded to a certain extent. He gave me two painkillers or rather injections, and then he addressed my wife and told her, "Jelena, the best thing for you to do would be to go to Belgrade." He knew that I had an aunt, my father's sister, who lived in Belgrade. He went to see whether there were any trains running to Belgrade on that day, and the trains were still running to Zagreb, Ljubljana, Vinkovci, Belgrade, and further on. He returned to fetch us and he told us, "There is a train leaving in half an hour. There is nobody there. The train will probably be empty. Let me take you there." He did take us to the railway station. He bought us tickets. We got on the train and we started our journey. There was another dangerous point that we had to cross and that was Stari Jankovci. The railway track goes through there and that was where international trains were always stopped. ZNG members controlled the passengers on all the trains there. They entered the compartments. They inspected papers. I heard that things like that happened. Sometimes they would take the people off the trains and those people would be taken somewhere. I didn't know what happened to them thereafter. I don't know who those people were, but in any case there were rumours. But I know for a fact that the trains were stopped in Jankovci and that happened to the train that we were on. I was seated next to the window. A three- or four-man strong patrol came, including a young man who recognised my wife. He told her, "Teacher, what are you doing here?" And then he saw me. It was clear to him that we were actually leaving the area. He held at both sides of the door literally blocking the view from anyone outside. His mates came along he told them, "Move along, things are fine here." He bid us farewell and went on. In Sid when we crossed into Serbia, I was addressed by a man who was part of the official escort of the train, and he said, "I saw you on the train. What's wrong with you?" As I couldn't speak my wife said that we had had some problems since she did not know who he was. He asked whether he should stop the train or if we were able to go on. And I waved my hand to show him that we can go on. By way of radio he called someone in Belgrade and we arrived there. There was an ambulance and a police patrol awaiting us. I was placed in the ambulance while my wife picked up our two children and went to my aunt's place. I was taken to the emergency ward. I was operated on there and the -- and I was bandaged. My shoulder was put back in place. My palate was stitched, and I stayed three days in the ward. Later on, I went to my aunt's apartment where I was treated at home. A nurse would come every day and for five days I received infusion because I was unable to eat. I was blue all over, and I received vaccines to prevent blood clotting. After some ten days, I started walking with a stick and my condition improved significantly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Susa, how long have you known Mr. Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: I met Goran Hadzic in 1973. I was in the second year of high school, whereas he had just started high school. We were introduced to each other through our colleague, Ms. Zivka.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not hear the last name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They liked each other at the time. We simply started socialising. We did not become exceptionally good friends, but I have known him since that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Following your education were you still in contact with him?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Yes. Although not as intensively. Whereas I studied law, he studied economics, and we ran into each other occasionally in Osijek. He did not seem to attend all of the classes at his university but that was the nature of his studies. In any case, we travelled together when we went back home because we stayed in Osijek during the week. When he started working in the same company where his father had worked before retirement, we would see each other. I was a hunter and Goran bred some dogs and we therefore had some common topics. I think the families visited each other, say, every six months or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: During the period where interethnic tensions were being raised in Croatia, did you have contact with Goran Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Please explain.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: I read in the newspapers that following an incident at Plitvice, Goran was arrested. As far as I could tell from the article, on their return from Knin they stopped at the Plitvice national park where he was arrested. He was taken to Zagreb and then released after a while to go home to Pacetin. He also experienced beatings. My wife and I sat in our car and went to visit him. When I went to Pacetin to see him, it was registered because before we joined the road between Vinkovci and Vukovar, one needs to turn towards Pacetin, and there was a Croatian check-point there. I was stopped and one of the people asked me where we were going. I showed him my official ID, and he asked me, "Mr. Prosecutor, what is your business in that Chetnik village?" Because you had to let them know you were going to turn to Pacetin. Between the barricade and the village, there was perhaps some 150 metres and unless you had previously announced your intention, you may be fired at. I told him that I was going to visit a friend. I didn't say it was Goran Hadzic. I just told him that I had a sick friend. And he said yeah, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Perhaps this is the result of very open nature of the questions asked by Mr. Zivanovic, but this whole topic of what happened I do not believe was anywhere in this witness's statements or -- and in the proofing notes, and so the Prosecution is unawares of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what part is not in the statement, and why it is relevant is because it is viva voce witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, the issue is notice. Well, we were not aware that this witness was going to talk about this particular incident, and it should have been at least in the witness summary or in the proofing note or in the 50-some-page statement that this witness provided. But it's nowhere to be found.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: If it is related to this particular incident as to visit to Goran Hadzic in Pacetin, we didn't spoke about it. It is first time that I hear from the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: You may -- you may move on -- you may continue, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please go on. You were explaining your trip.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Yes, I stopped at some point. I apologise. I have so many things in my memory and stories to that did not make their way into the statement but I'll try to stick to the statement itself. I was under an obligation to submit a report to the prosecutor's office on my visit to Mr. Hadzic and what I did there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you another thing since you are testifying under oath. You are not only limited in your testimony to the content of your statement. Should you remember anything else that is true and accurate and of importance for the proceedings, you have to tell us irrespective of what is contained in the statement.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Everything I've said so far is true, although it is not up to me to estimate the weight of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you arrived Belgrade, did you have occasion to see Goran Hadzic in the period after that?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Yes, I saw him only once in the home foundation in Belgrade in Nusiceva Street. He asked me then whether I was willing to assume the position of -- in a particular body, although he still didn't know what its name was going to be. He just said that it was supposed to be some kind of centre for civilian affairs in the region. I answered to him that I had already discussed it with Koncarevic and that I was willing to take up that position. I wanted to say that he wasn't at the home foundation to see me. He just spoke to me for a few minutes and he also greeted my wife who was present. He was accompanied by Vitomir Devetak whom I did not know at the time. Later on we were introduced and then I put two and two together and I realised I had seen him before at the home foundation. In any case, they were on their way to a meeting and we only exchanged a few words.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I see the clock.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. Mr. Susa, we take our first break, 30 minutes, so we will be back at 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Susa, did you hear of the existence of the Serb National Council?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: I did, when I was still in Vinkovci. I could read it in the newspapers that the Serbian National Council was established and one could also read about the members. I only knew some of them who had been prominent experts in the fields of culture, education, and alike, and who were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you a member of the Serb National Council?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: No, I was never a member of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear about a decision of the Assembly of SBWS from 1991? It was decided that the government of the SBWS be established. The date was the 25th of June, 1991.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: I heard about it when I was in Belgrade. I had no information about the session itself and the decisions reached there until later.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you left for Belgrade, when did you again go to the territory of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: I returned for the first time in August 1991 after there was preliminary discussion with me about assuming a position in that body that was supposed to be established for the SBWS. That is when I went to Dalj with a group of friends and associates.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Who formed the group of your colleagues and friends, and who did you discuss the proposition before going to Dalj?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Before that there was a conversation in Brane Crncevic's office. Mr. Ilija Koncarevic was present during the conversation as well as Mr. Dusan Pekic, retired general. Then I met the people who were there for the first time. There was also Mr. Simonovic who was the secretary of the federal assembly. Mr. Crncevic asked me, and he was the first one to ask me then, whether I would be willing to assume that position. It all happened before I met Mr. Hadzic at the same place which followed a few days later. I told him that I had no means to support my family and that my circumstances were changed. I had a very serious plan to leave Serbia altogether and to accompany my friend Tomo Ilic to Sidney, Australia. Mr. Crncevic told me that this technical issue of income could be dealt with because he would be of assistance in order for me to find a job and that under such circumstances I would be willing to assume that position. After he said that, I agreed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us how you reached Dalj?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: We used the road from Novi Sad, through a number of settlements, including Srpski Miletic. Then one arrives at a bridge across the Danube in order to reach Erdut. Erdut is the first settlement after the border in Croatia. The next settlement in line is Dalj. That was the route we took.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any check-points along the route to Dalj?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: The leg through Serbia, I think it is Bogojevo that is on the other side of the bridge, that is where the first check-point was manned by Serb police. We had our IDs checked and we were let through. When we crossed the bridge when we reached the fork to Erdut, there was another check-point which at that time was of mixed composition. When I say that, I mean to say that there were some policemen as well as JNA members there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Had you been in Dalj before that?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: No, never before.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Where did you go? What -- what location in Dalj?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: To the centre of town where there are several buildings. The building we entered and the building where we met was the building of the village library or the town library.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Who did you meet in Dalj on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: I saw Goran Hadzic there. He was the only one I knew there with the exception of a number of judges, colleagues, and prosecutors who were from Vukovar who, for some other places, were in Dalj that day as well. The colleagues who worked in Vukovar included a colleague who used to work in Osijek, and I knew him in our regular work. Ilija Koncarevic was there, whom I met previously at Mr. Crncevic's, and also Mr. Bogdan Vojnovic came with me together from the direction of Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have the opportunity to meet any members of the future government in Dalj that time?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: As I said, there were a number of them there. Maybe ten or fifteen. And that was where I met Mr. Vitomir Devetak again. I'd seen him before. I met Boro Milinkovic. Dr. Jovic. Dr. Mladen Hadzic. I don't know if I saw anybody else there. I cannot remember. I probably did, but I cannot remember their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And are you able to tell us if you met Radovan Stojicic, Badza, if that was the first time or whether you had met him before?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: On that day in Dalj when I saw him, I wasn't quite sure. I didn't know exactly who that was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: That was a very leading question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, we have -- we have the answer now. So move on but be careful.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I really don't know how to put the question to the witness if he met some particular person. I must tell the name of this -- that person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understood your question as being whether I met any people there that I'd worked with before, but it wasn't just those people who were there in the Dalj library. There was some other people there, people in military uniforms, people who evidently belonged to some other formation. When you specifically asked me about Radovan Stojicic, Badza, at the point in time when I saw him in Dalj - and I did see him in Dalj - I didn't know what his function was. At one point a number of people in uniform appeared. These were brown uniforms. I don't know how to describe them. They were modern, brown, war combat military uniforms. This was a group of people that I learned was from Vukovar. There were two brothers. I think they were twins and that their last name was Lazic, and there was evidently somebody there who was leading them and that is how they were sitting at the table and that was the first time that I saw Radovan Stojicic, Badza. Later I got to meet him. But I knew when the first time was that I saw him and I didn't communicate with him then.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember if then or later possibly you had the opportunity to see anyone else, any of his associates perhaps?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: All the people who appeared in Dalj then appeared several times later in places where I happened to be as well. I think that during the next ten days this contact or scene, Badza and people who were there in that group, was something that occurred more frequently. I think for the second time in Erdut, when I saw Radovan Stojicic, Badza, he was in the company of Mr. Zavisic, whom I knew as a high-ranking Serbian operative who I used to meet in Novi Sad, and I think that was the first time in my life that I saw Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And did you know who Radovan Stojicic, Badza, was at that time or can you tell us what you knew at that time?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: When I met him for the first time I didn't know almost anything about him. When you meet people in gatherings, you would ask who is that person, who is that person, and those people are asking about you as well. Already on the way back to Belgrade, the people who were there with me, Milos Vojnovic, Bogdan Vojnovic, they told me that this was a very high-ranking member of the Serbian MUP. I knew that of Zavisic. Let me just remind you that at that point when I went to Dalj I myself had began to work in the Serbian MUP as an inspector, independent inspector for economic crimes, and that is the work that Mr. Crncevic said he could fix for me. I received a very high salary for the conditions at the time. I had social insurance. My wife was able to draw on the salary through my bank account, and I was happy that my family was taken care of and I could do some other things. In the city secretariat in Novi Sad when I went to collect the decision about my new post, that was when I met Mr. Zavisic. Before that, I didn't -- I didn't know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you also saw Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan. Can you tell me at that time, did you have any information about him, who he was?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: I had information already from the time I was in Vinkovci, this is very indirect information acquired through the media, where there was talk about how he was captured in Croatia while smuggling arms and there was some kind of court proceedings against him in Zagreb. I think that only a few times before that I had heard of Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan. Of course, later I became more interested and I saw who he was and where he was from and what were all the things that he was involved in.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And could you please tell us how people in Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem viewed the arrival of Radovan Stojicic, Badza, and the group of policemen who came with him? How did they see that?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: What can I tell you? When you're in danger, when you're afraid for your life, when somebody comes to help you and when that someone is either a representative of Serbia or of the federal organs, then for you that represents a certain relief.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And do you know how Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, was viewed?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Well, just like myself people knew very little about Arkan. When he appeared, he brought men with him who appeared like serious soldiers. This was not just a group of people assembled from the street. Already by the way they appeared, by the way they talked, by their conduct, one could conclude that these were members of some serious military formation. Later, getting to know everything that he was involved in better and who all these people were, I received confirmation for this assumption. All of these people were people who completed military schools in other countries. Some of them perhaps in Serbia. They were highly educated soldiers, able to use the latest equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And Arkan and the group that came with him, did they take part in combat; do you know?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Yes, they did participate in combat. They did not carry out any political work in the field. They carried out activities that have to do with military operations in the -- in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us, do you remember when you were elected into the government of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem and what was the post that you were appointed to?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: The Great National Assembly in its session in September, at the proposal of the prime minister-designate Goran Hadzic, selected a government in which I was given the post of minister for justice.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember if Radovan Stojicic, Badza, ever attended these government sessions?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Yes. Not each one. He would come from time to time. He was a person of a few words. He would sit. Sometimes he would talk about losses in the field, about how serious they were. He did not ever propose anything specific or ask us for any opinions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did he inform you about military operations, about future plans?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: No, never. We did not take part in the drafting of any operational plans, and after actions were carried out he never informed us about the course of those actions. He would stick to a kind of statistical line where he would talk about the casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did Radovan Stojicic, Badza, ever issue any instructions, directives? Did he ever reach any decisions about any specific problem or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: No. No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether Radovan Stojicic, Badza, ever had any functions in Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Radovan Stojicic, Badza, was the commander of the Territorial Defence of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who appointed him to that post?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Yes, I know who appointed him indirectly. He was appointed to that function by Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "Serbia," what do you mean more specifically?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Well, look, at that time the authority of Serbia and organs of the SFRY were overlapping in certain aspects. So he was sent to us to head the Territorial Defence. I believed, and I believe that now, that somebody from the federal organs, or Serbia, was behind that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And do you know if the government of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem adopted a decision appointing Radovan Stojicic, Badza, to that post?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: No. Perhaps that's a bit unusual, but as far as police and military structures, we did not make any strategic decisions, executive decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And do you know if perhaps the Assembly of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem perhaps made such a decision?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Well, as far as I know, it did not, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And did Goran Hadzic himself perhaps make that decision ; do you know?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: No, no. I don't think Goran Hadzic would make that decision by himself. It was something that would be made by the government or by the assembly, but the documents that I had indicate that this was not something that was discussed either by the government or by the assembly nor by Goran Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember if Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, attended government meetings?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Yes, he did. More rarely than Radovan Stojicic, Badza. He would come. Sometimes he would be in the hall in entrance to the room where the government sessions were, and sometimes he would be present at these sessions. As opposed to Radovan Stojicic, Badza, he was well-known. He was loud. He would always speak with his voice raised. He would always be discussing something with someone. I didn't really have any frequent contacts with him. I practically had no contacts with him, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And at these government session, did he issue any instructions, directives, make proposals to what the government was supposed to do, adopt, things like that?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us, if you know, what the relationship was between Radovan Stojicic, Badza, and Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Like I said, Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, was a specific figure. You could not make a -- make an impression on him unless you held him in awe. But I think Radovan Stojicic, Badza, was the only person he held in awe. I must said that he had frequent conflicts with mostly two people: Slavko Dokmanovic, late Slavko Dokmanovic, and Boro Bogunovic. Slavko Dokmanovic irritated him because of one thing and that was because Slavko Dokmanovic consumed a little bit more alcohol and he was always slightly inebriated and this is something that really irritated Zeljko Raznjatovic, and he told him that several times in the presence of others including my own. He did not consider Boro Bogunovic as a serious man. He would always ironically say, "Where are you, minister? You're not to be seen anywhere. What service are you heading?" And this unfortunately was true because Boro Bogunovic was very rarely in Erdut. He would always find reasons why he wasn't there. And in principle he was not really a very capable person able to carry out the duties he was given. And during one such conflict with Dokmanovic when Dokmanovic was asking something of Raznjatovic, he wanted Raznjatovic to explain something to him, I didn't understand what the thing was about any way, Arkan started shouting at him and said, "Nobody can ask me about anything here. I don't have to account for my behaviour to anyone. The only person I can report to is Radovan Stojicic, Badza. So please remember that." Nobody ever asked him to report or do anything like that, but generally this applied to everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You have just mentioned Boro Bogunovic and you said that he attended government session very rarely. Where was his office while he was the minister of the interior?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: He would always be at the wrong place at the wrong time. You couldn't find him when you needed him most. Officially he was in Sid. The distance between Sid and Erdut was half a day at that time. For him that was always a good excuse for not coming to Erdut as often as he should have.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to show you a document that we were provided with concerning Radovan Stojicic, Badza, and Zavisic whom you also mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is 1D2206, tab 687. And it should not be broadcasted. Just to be on the safe side, I would propose to move to the private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, as far as you know, where was Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, deployed from the moment he arrived in SBWS?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: As far as I know, the first destination where Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, appeared was the village of Tenja, near Osijek. After his deployment in Tenja, and according to some information that was the result of a conflict with the local leader Jovan Rebraca, Zeljko Raznjatovic appeared in Erdut.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: How did you learn that Zeljko Raznjatovic appeared in Erdut?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: I have indirect information. Namely, I travelled from Belgrade to Erdut all the time, that was tiring and not very practical, because I had to work and I had a serious job. I didn't have a place to work. I didn't have an office. At one point I turned to Goran Hadzic, I talked to him about my problem, and then he told me, Mr. Vojnovic, and two other ministers to go and take up offices in the administrative building of the winery. And that was across the road from the building where we held our government sessions. We went there, we inspected the premises, those were well presented and fit for office work. I took two offices, I believe, Mr. Bogdan Vojnovic took one, and there was somebody else with us, either Caslav Otic or somebody else, and he took one or two offices. There was not much by way of office equipment. There was just a desk and a chair. We needed machinery. We needed a fax machine, we needed a copier. That's why we decided that we would go back to Belgrade and the next time we were to come we would bring everything with us. That was a decision that we followed through. We appeared in Erdut perhaps a couple of days later. My driver went to unload the van where all those things were, and then he returned, he said our offices were not there. I didn't understand. And then I went there and I realised that the entire winery was taken by the units that I'd not seen before, again impeccably dressed in military uniforms. I saw that military discipline ruled supreme there. I realised that Arkan took up all the premises. I went to see Goran. I complained. And then he said, "Leave it be. We can't deal with the problem at the moment. Leave the things that you had brought in an adjacent room. They will be safe there. In a couple of days we will find some other premises for you." And that's how the whole thing ended. Yes, I learned that Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, had arrived with his unit and occupied the entire building. That's what I learned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Had he gone to the government asking for such premises to be provided to him?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: I have to tell you, when Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, needed something and -- and explained that those things were needed for defence and for the purpose of war operations, he didn't request. He didn't beg. He just took things and used them. And that went without saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Radovan Stojicic, Badza, also came to those premises with his men. Do you know if he had turned to the government asking for premises? Did he ask for a permission to take up some of those rooms?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's leading. The first part of the question was assuming facts not in evidence. This witness has not testified about Badza coming to that location. And the second part is somewhat less leading but nevertheless still leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It seems that the first part of my question is not properly translated. I -- I asked when Radovan Stojicic, Badza, came not to those premises but in Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem generally, not in the premises. I didn't mention premises. So my question --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will repeat my question, sir. When Radovan Stojicic, Badza, arrived in SBWS, did he turn to the government and asked for a permission to take up a location with his men?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: I understood your question the first time round. Radovan Stojicic, Badza, just like Arkan, did not ask for any permissions. Let me just explain: Arkan and Badza did not share that location.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that when you first arrived in Croatia after you had fled Vinkovci that you found that JNA units that they manned check-points there. When it comes to the JNA and those units, did they ever turn to the government of the SBWS looking for accommodation in their -- in the area?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: No, never. In keeping with the prevalent regulations, they didn't even have to. In a situation when arms are used, a military can requisition assets for their purposes. That was part of our law. They could take whatever they needed against a certificate on the temporary expropriation of assets, and there was nobody who could forbid them to do that. They never asked for any such permission from us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you mentioned laws and regulations, did they apply only to the military or to any military formations?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Any military formations. The daily procedures are applied by the police who are always in a position to prevent crimes or destruction of evidence. This goes without saying and there's nothing in dispute about that among the legal profession.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Goran Hadzic gave that centre in Erdut to Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, to be used by his unit for training?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: I don't know that that was the case. How should I put it? Nobody could give Arkan anything and that includes Goran Hadzic. Goran Hadzic was in charge of some civilian activities, programmes and plans, and any assets in that respect. Anything that had to do with military strategy or military defence. There was nobody who could forbid anything to those persons who had been deployed in the area to defend us and to engage in military activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see, please, tab 628. It is P194.140.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You had an opportunity to see this document before. My first question about this document is this. Please look at the upper left corner. What you can see here is the Secretariat of President. Was there a secretariat of that kind within the government of the SBWS? Was there a secretariat of the prime minister or the president of the government.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: The government did have a secretariat, the secretariat of the government headed by Mr. Jovan Pejakovic. I never heard that the president had his own secretariat, not in our conditions, and in that sense this order leaves a lot to be desired. It doesn't make sense that Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, is appointed as a TO centre and a commander. That may be correct but then it wouldn't be signed by President Hadzic but by the commander of the TO, Radovan Stojicic, Badza.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We see a reference to staff commanders. Can you tell us if such positions existed? Were there any such staffs at the time in existence; and, if so, can you tell us what kind of staffs they were?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: It would be very pretentious to discuss any kind of staffs or the Territorial Defence, at least not to the extent its structure should look like. We have touched upon this earlier. In villages where there was a Serb majority, people self-organised and established village guards. They never assumed any type of organisation that would include commands and staffs. There was very little organisation in the process and much chaos. I didn't even know that on 21st September, 1991, there were any TO Staffs. I never saw that in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In the upper left-hand corner, you see a number, 1/91, followed by the date. To your knowledge, were there ever cases where different documents would be filed under the same number?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: No, that did not happen. I do have to say that Mr. Pejakovic was a very pedantic and precise person in how he kept records of all government documents. He would not have made that kind of mistake, and even if some mistakes happened, at the very first session of the government he would have it corrected as part of the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as you know, when did Mr. Pejakovic assume his duty, in real terms?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: I came to Dalj in August 1991 for the first time. It was also a consequence of the fact that Mr. Dukovic was supposed to be appointed government secretary. However, Mr. Dukovic did not enjoy the support of his own village, Borovo Selo. He left Borovo Selo for Belgrade and the people there held it against him.
