Goran did initially accept that Mr. Dukovic be the government secretary, but then he told me that the local population did not want him and suggested Mr. Pejakovic instead who was a lawyer. So even then we agree that Mr. Pejakovic would be the government secretary and he was appointed to that position at the next government session.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did he begin performing those tasks before his appointment?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Yes. But he was only formally appointed at the assembly session. In real terms, he began filing records and creating the files before that. He put the whole system in place that was supposed to monitor all government communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see, please, P3217, tab 710.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't see this. This is much better.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is a proclamation of general mobilisation. I won't go into the contents. I would only ask you to -- draw your attention to the heading in the upper left-hand side corner. Again, we see the same number, 1/91. The document is dated the 23rd of August, 1991, in Dalj. That is precisely what I wanted to ask you. To your knowledge, this document and the preceding one you saw on the screen, could they have been filed under the same number?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: They should not have been. As regards the proclamation, I am aware of its contents and I assisted in drafting it. The time-period does seem to tally, although I cannot be a hundred per cent certain. But as for the number of the document, 1/91, that would seem to be correct because at the time we were busy mobilising people, and I also see that it was issued by the prime minister. In any case, we were all aware of it by the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us now go back to document --

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: I have to point out one very important thing. At this point in time, on 23rd of August, 1991, Goran Hadzic was still not the prime minister formally speaking. It was well-known that he was going to assume that duty, but due to the urgency of this matter the document had to be drafted as such in order for it to be signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us go back to the previous document, tab 628. It is P194.140.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether Goran Hadzic ever issued documents in the form of orders?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: No. As per law and in keeping with his authority, he was not in a position to issue orders. One had to be commander to issue orders, whereas he was not that. He mainly used decisions within the remit of the prime minister and the government itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you returned in August and subsequently in 1991, what was the situation like in SBWS? What kind of living conditions prevailed?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Difficult ones. As early as June 1991, after tensions were raised and communications ceased between Serb and Croatian villages, the Croatian side cut off electricity. It is a big problem because the electric network was also connected to water supply because of the pumps -- pumps that were used. There was also a shortage of oil and gasoline, commodities such as sugar, salt, flour, they were all lacking and it all contributed to poor living conditions for ordinary people.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What was the situation like with the JNA members in the district at the time? And how many were there?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Their numbers increased constantly because the intensity of the conflict grew. In that situation, Croatian paramilitary formations attacked barracks, surrounding them, cutting off electricity and water supply, and cutting off supply lines, in terms of food, for the armed forces. At the same time, they increased attacks resulting in a number of killed and wounded soldiers. At that time in the SBWS, the number of JNA soldiers was on the increase. They were mostly people who were mobilised. For years before that there was a trend within the JNA that young people, having graduated from high school, would serve their military term before embarking upon their studies at universities. In other words, there were very few serious active-duty soldiers equipped to wage war. In such a situation, units were manned through the process of mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you something about the authority of the government, but for the time being I'd like to focus only on Stojicic, Badza, and the people he brought with him, as well as Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, and his group. Did the government have any legal or factual authority to order anything to Stojicic, Badza, or Raznjatovic, Arkan? Could it order them to do something or not to do something?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: I think I have already answered that question. Let me repeat. There was no possibility for the government as a whole, as well as Goran Hadzic individually, to order anything to the two people in question or to prohibit them from doing anything. Anyone who spent more than a day there was in a position to see that for themselves. As a government member, I never took part in issuing a single decision that would order those people to do something or request anything of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did the government have any factual ability to use force to, say, have Radovan Stojicic and his group or Raznjatovic, Arkan, and his group removed from the area of the SBWS?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Even if someone had wanted to do something like that, you would have needed a much stronger force than they had. I have to tell you, though, that we had no force at our disposal whatsoever. Perhaps the odd government member did have a side-arm but no one was very skilful in soldierly skills. A few of us had drivers or security escort and we did have a team of guards that guarded the government premises round the clock. Perhaps there was a dozen of them, but I doubt they were any more capable in -- in military sense than the rest of us ordinary people. In other words, we had no possibility to prohibit anything to these two or to have them removed from the area unless they wanted to do so themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What kind of relationship was there between Stojicic, Badza, and the JNA and its officers?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Their relationship was excellent. They all co-ordinated their activities, as far as I could see. They held daily meetings where reports were submitted, attended by Stojicic and Arkan or one of his men and JNA representatives. Their command was in Erdut. It is well known that Arkan was on exceptionally good terms with General -- I can't recall his last name off the cuff. His last name begins with a B. He was killed later on. Yes, Bratic, General Bratic. Later on, he had the same kind of relationship with Biorcevic. As for Stojicic, Badza, he was in daily contact -- well, there was a room in Erdut that we had to passes by en route to our government offices. We would frequently see them in the yard where they stood and we would great them before moving on to our premises.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us something about the work of the government itself. Who presided over the government sessions?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: If Goran Hadzic was present, he presided. In his absence, it was basically done by Dr. Mladen Hadzic. The two of them are not related, despite the fact that they share the last -- the same last name. We preferred Goran Hadzic presiding because then things were dealt with briefly. When Dr. Hadzic presided, such meetings would usually turn into much talk on his own about things that mostly concerned himself and lasted for several hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Was there a condition that had to be met before a government session would be considered a proper session?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Yes, of course. We had to have a sufficient number of ministers in order to be able to discuss and decide. We were quarried if we had 50 per cent plus 1. Otherwise, say, three people met, they could discuss things, but whatever they decided was not binding on anyone. Also all decisions were voted on. That is why it was important that we were present in sufficient numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And how were the government meetings prepared? Can you remember?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Yes, I can remember. At the very beginning, perhaps for the first 15 or 20 days until things got going, it was a little bit improvised. At the meeting itself somebody would be adding items to the agenda, but very quickly a rule was introduced that each minister who wanted to have an item placed on the agenda would have to notify the rest of us about the topic that he wanted to be placed on the agenda. And then the secretariat would provide this material in a sufficient number of copies for all the ministers so that they could prepare for each item on the agenda. Only exceptionally when we were discussing very difficult life problems could that be added to the agenda during the meeting itself. Otherwise, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any notes made during the government meetings?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Yes, of course. There was a record made. The meeting would finish with a recording of everything that happened. There would be a summary of all the conclusions and positions that were important. There would be separate parts on the decision-making and the result of votes, and then this part with these conclusions would be provided to everybody at the beginning of every next meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: From the point in time when the government was made and for as long as the government of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem existed, are you able to tell us what the situation was regarding movements around the area, in view of the authority you had as members of the government?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Well, at some point after the first 15 or 20 days of work, we were given official IDs where our identity was stated. These were official passes signed by Goran Hadzic and with the stamp of the government. However, very often these official IDs or passes were not enough to let us into the area of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. To be more precise, it depended on which side you wanted to enter. If you were entering through Bogojevo to Erdut, which was the entrance we used most frequently, where we were known, we would pass through easily. But if you wanted to enter through Negoslavci from the direction of Sid, you could not enter with that pass. You had to have a clear identifiable permit by the military authorities. This was a piece of paper with your particulars, the vehicle you were using, the direction you were moving in, on the paper and these were permits that were only valid for one day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic, I see the time as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Susa, we will take the second break, 30 minutes as well. We'll be back at 12.45.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Susa, could you just tell us briefly about the communications of the government within Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. Let's start with Vukovar, for example. Did the government have any communication with Vukovar in that period, from September, October, November, when the military operations were under way?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: As you yourself say, extensive, very complicated, and serious military operations were under way in Vukovar. We didn't go to Vukovar and we practically had no contact with them other than some indirect information from people who just happened to go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And are you able to tell us about the government's communications with Western Srem, with that area?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Until the army broke through towards that area, Sid, Tovarnik, towards Mirkovci, and to the right towards Lovas, Negoslavci, the communication there was very difficult. Let me put it differently. We had good communication with Baranja and along the direction from Bogojevo including Erdut and Dalj. That would be the limited area of our movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the village guards in certain Serbian villages. Are you able to tell us if the government had any communication with those village guards?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: There was communication from time to time. We didn't go there. Certain people from the villages which were encircled would manage to come out under exceptionally difficult circumstances along roads that were known to them, and they would come to Erdut from time to time. They would mainly come because of complex great problems they had in their villages. I'm repeating. There were electricity, water cuts, basic foodstuffs were lacking. There were no medicines. They were fighting epidemics and different illnesses, and that's why they would come, asking for help on these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: These village guards, was there any kind of unified command for them, if you know?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: As far as we are concerned, no, there wasn't anything like. Then later, Radovan Stojicic, Badza, managed to unify them. Until he came to the area, we were not any kind of command for them. We didn't present ourselves in that way either.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "we," who do you mean?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: I'm thinking of the government based in Erdut.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us anything about the relationship of the village guards and the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: In the beginning, all of those people living in that area were very relieved when the Yugoslav People's Army came. If we're talking about ordinary people, they felt like that later too. However, individuals from these village guards which imposed themselves as leaders in a particular village slowly came into conflict and in collision with members of the JNA who were giving them certain assignments that they were not willing to carry out. On the other hand, they still had the obligation towards the people who had chosen them by acclamation to lead them in the defence of their villages. When they would appear before these local leaders with requests for help with their living problems, they, as a rule, didn't have any response or answer to these problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The Assembly and the government of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, did they make any decisions in relation to these village guards?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: No. As far as I know, they did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did the government or the prime minister ever issue any orders to these village guards as to what they were to do?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: This was impossible, in practice and by the letter of the law. These people were villagers. They were mostly people that we knew from before. And in the first stage, that I would even limit to the first year, did not even consider us as somebody to whom they would be answerable to or from whom they could receive orders. These people were our equals, more or less, and we were on the one hand, privileged because we were not on the front lines and we were not in daily danger of losing our lives. The authority that we could exercise in relation to them was never established in the first place and it was not something that was seriously discussed of. We constantly tried by words or personal engagement to help them, to provide essential medications for them, to provide doctors there. There were people with influenza, children's illnesses, infectious diseases which if you didn't control you would have considerably serious circumstances, which was something that did happen in certain villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know in the Assembly of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem made any decisions regarding the Territorial Defence of the area and their joining the armed forces of the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: That is a good question. Had someone been making decisions regarding the TO, it could only have been the assembly, and as far as I know the assembly did not make any decisions relating to the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We have a document here that I would like you to look at.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is L19, tab 601.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm familiar with the contents of this decision. I didn't understand your previous question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well perhaps my question was unclear. This decision in the lower part of the text and goes onto the following page, are you familiar with that decision of the 10th of October, 1991?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Yes. When you put the question to me about village guards and the Territorial Defence, I said that we did not make any decisions in the government or the assembly in terms of their formation or work. This is what Radovan Stojicic, Badza, did with his decisions that we didn't have any part in. Once they were conceived and formed in that way, at one point, it became clear that the Territorial Defence, for purposes of efficiency and problems in the field, have to be resubordinated to units of the Yugoslav People's Army. I first saw this concept at the government, and it was placed on the agenda by the late Ilija Koncarevic. I myself and everyone else was in favour of adopting this decision. I need to point out something important here. In relation to the existing provisions of federal laws and decisions of certain federal organs, primarily the decision of the Presidency on establishing or declaring imminent threat of war, this decision seems superfluous. However, under this decision we wanted to make it known that we ourselves were quite aware of the situation in the field and that the Territorial Defence had to be joined to the armed forces of the SFRY without fail.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us what the relationship between the government of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem and the Yugoslav People's Army was?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't define them as good relations. Why? There was a lot of lack of understanding of the other's rights and duties. We tried, at least in the later stage, to assert ourselves as those who made and implemented civilian decisions. The army simply did not wish to accept that, judging by their decisions. When did they address us? When, in certain areas, there were activities that were not classic combat activities, problems would become beyond what they could deal with. Then they would address us, ask us to repair the damage, and then when we would propose to them that we plan together and implement these actions at a later stage, they would remain passive and none of this would ever then be implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know if the JNA informed the government of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem about its activities?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: No, not officially. No reports were sent. It may have done in personal, private contacts, or if somebody learned something and then conveyed that knowledge to somebody else. But directly, it was not done.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that one needed a special permit to go from Sid to Negoslavci and that that special permit was issued to you. Who was it who issued those permits? Where were they obtained?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: In the centre of Sid there was a building, and in that building there was an office manned by two men. Maybe there were more than two but I remember those two because I communicated with them the most. Their names were Grahovac and Filipovic. They issued those permits which were sufficient for one to enter the area, to move about the area, and to return from the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did the JNA recognise those permits?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know if Grahovac, whom you have just mentioned, had a position in the government of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: No, he never turned up at the government in Erdut, nor did I hear that he was ever engaged on our behalf in any capacity.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did he [Realtime transcript read in error "you"] submit his reports to the government on what he was doing?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us just correct something. My question was whether "he" submitted reports and this was misrecorded. Did he submit reports to the government?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: I answered: No, he never submitted any reports to the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Was he perhaps an assist or a deputy of a minister?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: He did not have a position in the government as far as I know. If he had had a position, I'm sure I would have known.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did the government send any instructions or any such thing to that office in Sid which issued those permits; more specifically, to Mr. Grahovac or Filipovic?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: No -- no, not as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When the government arrived in Erdut, did it have a security detail, somebody who provided physical security?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Perhaps not on the first couple of days, and then some people appeared, all of them from Borovo Selo. I believe that I have already mentioned them. I don't know whether there were more than a dozen of them. They were on duty 24/7, two or three of them, and that was good because we had already installed some state-of-the-art equipment that somebody may have stolen. They provided physical security for the building where we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Who was in charge of organising that part of the tasks, providing security for the government building?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Nobody appeared officially based on a decision, but we all knew that he was -- that they were Stevo Bogic's friends from Borovo Selo. He was there all the time. They communicated with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know if Goran Hadzic had his own body-guards?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: I know because I personally knew all those men. One of them was Milenko Japundzic and the late ... I knew him from before the war. What's his -- Ljubo Modrinic. I apologise. He was my karate trainer for a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The men who provided security for the government building, were they also Goran Hadzic's personal body-guards at the time in 1991 and 1992? Was that one and the same service?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: What do you mean, one and the same service? No. Those people who were on the building provided security for the building. When we had drove to Baranja in several cars, whether they came with us, I don't know. I think that I saw them on several occasions in Baranja, but I'm not sure that they were anybody's body-guards. That was just not within their purview.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know if Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, was a member of the security detail for Goran Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: In technical terms, it was impossible. Arkan could not have been Goran's body-guard because Goran often travelled from Erdut to Novi Sad, Belgrade, and some other places to attend political meetings, while Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, stayed in Erdut with his unit. Every now and then Arkan would be heard saying that he guarded Goran, but he guarded every single one of us in that case, because he was only 200 metres away from us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the creation of an organisation known as the Serbian National Security?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Yes, I do. While I was waiting for a government session to begin, sitting with Ilija Koncarevic and Bogdan Vojnovic, Stevo Bogic approached us, we discussed some other things, and then he touched upon the topic or rather the need to create a service in a foreseeable future that would deal with national security and counter-intelligence. I realised that that was his desire. Ilija Koncarevic asked him whether he would be interested in doing that. He was a vice-president without a portfolio, so he was bored sitting in Erdut all day long. He said, "Yes, I'm thinking about that, but I don't know how to do it, how to go about it." And asked me and I agreed to make a draft of how such a service should look like. And also I -- I agreed to make a draft decision constituting that service and to make a draft of the inception document. I didn't want to go into the details such -- such as the number of personnel. And then Ilija Koncarevic, who was a former member of the military intelligence, told us, "Whatever you're planning, it is the assembly that has to make a decision." He said, "I don't know but what is going to do what he has just promised that he would?" It took me some ten or fifteen days to draw that necessary decision and to draft the form of that organisation and the personnel structure. I gave him some 20 pages of densely typed information. And then, after some ten days later, he told me, "You know, I read everything carefully and it looks very complicated. I don't think that I would be able to do that." And all that after I had adapted everything and said that the head of that service did not have to have any particular knowledge, that he could be a political figure. However, those who will be heads of sectors, departments, and managers, I thought that those people should have specific knowledge, specific skills, that they should have a university education, so he told me, "You know what, I can't ensure such people. You don't have such people in your bodies. Where am I supposed to find them?" Such draft or any specific proposal of that institution was never discussed at any of the government session. This simply remained a plan or simply an activity that he wanted to implement but never got around doing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: One more thing. From the moment when Radovan Stojicic, Badza, became the commander of the Territorial Defence of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, what was the relationship between the Territorial Defence and its units and the government? Was there any relationship at all? Were you in communication with each other?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: You mean all the units of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Some of the units.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: The contacts that we had with particular units got lost, and when their representative attended a government session, that representative would be exclusively Badza, nobody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You were appointed a minister of justice and administration in the government of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. What were the main tasks and duties of your ministry? What was its purview?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: My ministry, first and foremost, had to draft basic documents that served to establish judiciary bodies. It was a complex procedure that we had to implement within a very short space of time. I would like to emphasise Mr. Vojnovic, Stankovic, and Ajdukovic's contribution, and a group of professional and highly professional individuals who belonged to the justice system of Serbia and the Federal Assembly of Yugoslavia. They assisted us in implementing that task in record time. They provided us with their expertise, know-how, and technical capabilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether the Ministry of Justice prepared the constitutional law of the Serbian region of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Generally speaking, we adopted that as our own document, as our own proposal to the Great National Council. Nobody was a big enough expert to do that. Milos Vojnovic takes most credit for drafting that and I was just his assistant.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see please L1. It is tab 589. Second page. It -- the translation does not correspond to the original text. Oh, sorry, third page of English translation, please. Fourth. Fourth page of English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll withdraw the question because I don't know the exact page. My next question is this: Did your ministry prepare the Law on the Implementation of the Constitutional Law?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see, please, P1808. It is tab 560.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please look at Article 1 where it says that: "The laws of the Republic of Croatia would no longer be applicable." Why was that? Why were the laws and regulations of Republic of Croatia no longer valid in Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: As I have already stated, after the HDZ won in the multi-party elections, drastic changes affected all spheres of life. One of those spheres was the legal system. The Serbs were removed from the constitution as a constituent people. Many other laws and regulations were no longer acceptable if for no other reason than for the fact that the Serbs had not participated in their passing by the parliament. Therefore, it was necessary to make the legal practice of Croatia ineffective because we were in no position to know what would happen in the future period. In view of everything that was going on in Croatia at the moment, this was indispensable. This was absolutely necessary, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And can you now please look at Article 3 of the same law.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: I can see it. I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It says here: "As of the day when the constitutional law comes into effect on the territory of the Serb region, all governmental bodies, bodies of local self-government, and other bodies and organisations of the Republic of Croatia shall terminate their work." At that time, were there any organs of the Republic of Croatia in that territory at the moment when this law was passed?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: A few months before that, they had withdrawn from the territory. There were no longer any bodies of the Republic of Croatia in place.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did the Ministry of Justice prepare and draft laws on ministries?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Yes. The Law on the Government, the Law on The Secretariat, all that was prepared by the Ministry of Justice.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: According to the Law on the Government that you mentioned, can you tell us who elected the prime minister and members of the government?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: I don't have the text before me, but they were elected by the Grand National Assembly. They were all elected separately, although the ministers were elected pursuant to a proposal made by the prime minister designate.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Who were the ministers answerable to?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: To the body that elected them, which was the National Assembly. Hence, the prime minister's remit was made narrower, and I will explain why. None of the bodies had been elected directly at elections, which was considered a shortcoming. That is why the prime minister could not receive the same authority that they otherwise have in different systems when such results are achieved in a different way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Who could remove a government member, including the prime minister?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: The Grand National Assembly could. If Goran Hadzic, as the prime minister, was dissatisfied with the work of a minister, he could not have them removed. He could only submit a report to the Grand National Assembly explaining his position, and then the Assembly, by virtue of its own decision, would perhaps have the minister removed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could the Grand National Assembly reject such a proposal?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Of course it could.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's look at L27, tab 608, which is the Law on the Government.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Article 8, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I still don't have Article 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is on the next page in the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: There it is.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Please look at paragraph 2 of Article 8. Please explain this provision under which, "A member of the government shall be responsible to the prime minister for representing and implementing the views of the government as well as for discharging the duties assigned or entrusted to him by the prime minister."

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: I think the second paragraph of article 2 is clear. Each one of us in the course of our work is answerable to the prime minister. We were duty-bound to implement everything that was put forth by the government as its joint position. However, there were some tasks that do not fall within the narrow limit or framework of each minister, but such a framework could be issued by the prime minister. If a government member did not meet his or her obligation, they could not be removed by the prime minister, but it is sufficient grounds to initiate a removal procedure before the Grand National Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Article 17, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Here, we see that the government shall supervise the work of ministries and other organisations. Did the government carry out such supervision over the work of the ministries?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: This was a general position envisaged for some better happier times when many professional staff were expected to work as part of the government. This was not the case at the time. Who could control and supervise the work of my ministry at the time? It was simply not a part of the times. It was not applied. It was not done. The ministers did submit periodic quarterly, semi-annually, and annually reports to the government which they drafted based on the specific issues for each of the ministries, and then these reports were adopted at assembly sessions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say periodic reporting, as far as I know, the government lasted for only five months.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Yes. So this was in principle. I think I submitted one joint report. Bogdan Vojnovic did the same on the state of finance. He did it rather more often than me. But as for others, I don't remember. In any case, no procedure of adoption or approval was undertaken that would be followed by a pass or fail mark for each of the ministries. It was simply a matter of need in order to have our colleagues informed of the problems we encounter and the solutions we come up with.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did ministers at sessions report on the work of their ministries; i.e., what was being done between two government sessions?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Well, of course, what else would be on the agenda? That is what we discussed. Some people were criticised because of the fact that they mainly reported orally, something that could not be monitored or followed. And at some point, they were made to put their reports in writing. So people would just come and start discussing a problem they have and ways to deal with it, but then it creates a problem with the secretariat because there's no specific decision, and then the secretariat had to draft it themselves. Later on, we pursued the policy of submitting everything in writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether the Ministry of the Judiciary drafted a law on measures in case of states of emergency?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: No, I don't think we worked on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether there ever was a state of emergency in the SBWS?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: I know there was a proposal drafted and presented by Mr. Slavko Dokmanovic. It had to do with some obligations to carry out farming work which was a significant issue. It did reach the assembly but it was not discussed at a session. No state of emergency was ever declared.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did the Ministry of Justice prepare a decision on the work and manner of work of municipal executive councils?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Yes, it was part of our -- of its basic remit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see, please, L53. It is tab 624.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We see the heading that the date was the 3rd of December, 1991. Was this decision implemented as proposed in the text?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Yes, partially, where it could have been implemented. There was still areas where we couldn't implement all that was contained in the decision. In any case, it was implemented partially. We appointed presidents of executive councils, and the executive councils then chose their own teams and notified us. We couldn't object to their choice because they chose the people they wanted to work with. The problems they had were significant, and, thus, we could not put forth any serious objections. Could the text be zoomed in, please. Otherwise I can't see.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: On the 3rd of December, 1991, or around that time, how did civilian authorities in the SBWS function?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Civilian authorities did not function fully because there was a constant overlap of competencies between us and the executive councils and the army in the field that had its own officers in charge of civilian affairs. Hence, civilian authorities always collided with the military in terms of who would be doing what. It usually ended up by the army offering its own interpretation, requesting that they give express approval. They may have had a legal basis, according to some federal regulation, but we hoped for better co-operation and more sensitivity for the situation in the field. However, it was not the case. Or let me be more precise. At this point in time, around December 3, 1991, in a number of areas, there was military rule. By definition, it poses significant problems for the functioning of executive councils.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Since there was military rule there, as you say, why was this decision issued in the first place, trying to establish civilian authorities?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: If one looks only at what is implementable at the time, you would never have adequate laws. We had to draft certain laws and measures for a period when such things would see the light of day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did the Ministry of Justice prepare a Law on Temporary Territorial Organisation of the SBWS and Temporary Local Self-Governance?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Yes, it was part of our basic remit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see, please, it is L1, page 29 to 33, tab 589.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is English page 84. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can see the date of this law.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Yes, the 22nd of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us go on to the next page. The next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We see here a list of municipalities and settlements. Do you recall how many municipalities were established under the law?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. Perhaps five or six. Well, there were as many as you can see in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: As for the system those five or six municipalities were organised in, was it implemented in the field?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Not as stipulated in the law. Because the temporary seat of Vinkovci municipality was in Mirkovci and for Osijek it was Tenja. But later on their names were changed by establishing the municipality of Mirkovci and of Tenja. In Article 10, there is a political presupposition, so to speak, reflecting our hope that in some future time we would also be able to include the towns of Vinkovci and Osijek in our territory. But at the moment of drafting this law already, we knew it was way too ambitious to expect. However, there was a school of thought or a number of people who insisted on it so that it reflects our wish. However, we quickly renamed them into the municipality of Mirkovci and the municipality of Tenja with the two towns being their seats.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Before this law was passed, was there another law or regulation that dealt with temporary territorial organisation and temporary local self-governance?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Not as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did the Ministry of Justice prepare the Law on The Interior?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: No. That law had been created in Belgrade and handed over to Mr. Bogunovic. If I recall well, it was presented by Sinisa Puskar on behalf of the ministry. I know it was drafted in Belgrade. I know so because later on Mr. Puskar joined my ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: As for the police force in SBWS, who commanded them? The police force, that is.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: They were under the command of a centre in Serbia. There was a large number of policemen who got work there. I myself was one of those people. And then they were transferred to different commands. But they were the ones who paid their salaries, provide their social benefits, their pension, and they were just temporarily deployed in Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you be a little more clear in your definition? Could you tell us in English what it means to be transferred to a different command, "otkomanda" [phoen], what does that mean that the policemen were sent to a different command?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: In the area of your home organ, you are registered as an authorised person, and then are you signed out in that place, you are transferred to a different location where you report to a different superior who will assign you tasks and activities. That does not mean that you lose your basic general status in the place where you began your employment. The fact that you are in a different area is a temporary matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So that means that a policeman who is in the Serbian MUP, for example, would be transferred to the MUP of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, for example?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: But he is not dismissed. At any point, he can be returned to Sombor, Novi Sad, Belgrade or to the place where he was originally from.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us who decides whether a person would be sent to Slavonia, Baranja, or Western Srem, or whether they would be sent back? Does the government Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem have any say in that?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: No. This is something that his police station or the city secretariat decides, depending on the case. In some cases, the agreement of the person was sought. It was not obligatory but some of them did want to return to the area where they were from originally by birth.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The justice ministry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, I would like to ask a clarifying question to the witness about the topic you touched upon. Your question was: "As for the police force in SBWS, who commanded them? The police force, that is." And the witness answered: "They were under the command of a centre in Serbia. There was a large number of policemen who got work there." And then, and this is what puzzles me a little bit: "I myself was one of those people." Do we have a translation problem or is that what the witness said and wanted to say? Mr. Witness, do you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand. I understand. Thank you for that warning. I said earlier that before I game to Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, I started to work at the city secretariat of the interior in Novi Sad as an independent inspector in the economic crimes department. I received my certificate about my temporary transfer to Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, and I was not given any more specific duties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And when was that? Could you give us a time-frame.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can tell you that it was in late August 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Zivanovic. Sorry for the interruption.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The justice ministry, did it prepare a decree on the temporary protection of the property of economic and private subjects of SBWS outside of the territory?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Yes, together with two other ministries, the Ministry of Finances and Ministry for the War Time Economy. I would say that the largest contribution was given by the finance ministry, by Mr. Bogdan Trifunovic [as interpreted], and then we made sure that then this was formed as a decision the way it should be.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not hear the very last words of the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Bogdan Vojnovic, not Bogdan Trifunovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: My question was complete actually. Okay. May we see, please, L18. It is tab 600.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the decree that we referred to. Could you please look at Article 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It's on the following page of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm looking at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And can you see here that special protection is planned. Could you explain to us a little more about this "special protection of property."

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: I have to tell that you the ownership structure in the former Yugoslavia, including Croatia, was mostly state-owned property. Private property had a very small proportion in the overall property categories. So when we were looking at certain forms of property ownership, very valuable property such as buildings, institutions, agricultural lands, banks, it was logical and normal for us to take over that property and to protect it because there was an objective danger that this property would be subject to misuse and that it would change the ownership structure in a way that would not be very specific and would become private in an impermissible way. So this was given special status. It became regional property which had to be recorded precisely and had to be protected. Above all, it had to be protected.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I think you've given a partial answer to my next question already, but still I will put the question to you. The justice ministry, did it prepare a decision on the temporary transfer of property of the Republic of Croatia, socially owned property, to the ownership of the SBWS?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Yes. I made a mistake when interpreting the previous decree. There are two decrees. Basically they boil down to the same thing. The first decree refers to property which is outside of the territory area. What does that mean? Of course, all property that was -- belonged to the Republic of Croatia originally was not located only in that area, SBWS. There was a lot of property of SBWS that was in Vojvodina, Serbia, inner Serbia, and Montenegro. So the first decree covers the property which was outside of the area which we also were taking over and placing under our protection. Specifically, we had a large problem with the Borovo chain stores. There were many of them in Serbia but we already knew that certain workers had tried to take that and present it as their own. This is something that had to be protected. There were also some holiday resorts in Montenegro and so on. Another part of the property which was in the area itself for the same reason was included under the decree and placed under our protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And this decision on the temporary transfer of property, this is tab 623, L52, are you able to tell us why it says that this is a temporary transfer of ownership?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Well, it's clear you could not definitely establish ownership. So something that was not subject to a broader interpretation and something that would not be well accepted by all and something -- well, we knew that in some future point in time the war would end, and then everybody would have to settle accounts with everybody else. Croatia would then say that, based on their investments, various forms of investments, including international loans, we owed them money for things that we had taken over. What we had taken over at that point in time was not definitely ours. It was temporarily placed under our protection. When all the problems were definitely resolved when relations would normalise, then we would proceed to establish rightful ownership.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: One more question relating to property regulations. Did your ministry prepare a decree on the temporary protection of abandoned property?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Yes. That segment includes two types of property: Socially owned and private property. Other than socially owned property, there are quite valuable pieces of private property. Houses, land, summer house, movable and immovable property. We did not want to place those things -- we did not want to have those things subject to abuse or misuse.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Abandoned property, are you able to tell us whether the decree could be implemented and to what degree could it have been implemented by the government?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: I'm thinking of courts. Perhaps we'll come to that and be able to additionally protect this property by that way. Unfortunately, we did not manage to implement this. For a number of reasons. For -- one of them is that there was lot of misuses in the field by individuals prone to crimes. It is particularly regrettable that we had a situation in which the JNA considered all property as war-booty and took a lot of that property out from the territory to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Personally, I had a lot of problems about this later.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May which see, please, L37. It is tab 615.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the decree that we referred to. What I would like to know now is -- well, the procedure is laid down here in these articles, from Article 1 onwards, the manner in which the property would be protected. What I would like to know is did other organs - you mentioned the JNA - that came there and practically had the power in the field, did they act in accordance with the decree and did they protect the property accordingly?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: I'm afraid that they did not. I've already said something about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And this property, was it made available to others for use? Was it sold? Was it given to somebody? I'm talking about the government of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: I understand your question. The ownership structure did not change in one single instance. Of course, property was given for temporary use. Newly formed work organisation and even private subject citizens were able, under specially set rules, get this property, be able to use it, care for it, make the required investments, and in the case of some profit they could have had earnings from it. But in essence, nobody could become an owner of something that they did not own before the war broke out.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Was the property given for others so that they could use it?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Yes, I've already said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Were any records kept of that?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Yes, records were kept. Quite proper records.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see please 1D1212. It is tab 258.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, could you repeat that. You were overlapping.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is 1D1212, tab 258.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I think that you've already seen this document. I'd like to know if this is one of the examples of these records. The document has a number of pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please look at the next page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I've seen all of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Is this one of the documents, a record of things that were being given for the temporary use?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Yes. These are drafts that were retyped. The contents are identical but they were typed and looked a little bit more orderly. This is property given to physical entities. This is agricultural land that had to be cultivated in any case, both for the benefit of the people who had its temporary use and also due to the fact that land that was not regularly cultivated could be damaged. It would be covered by weeds and it would deteriorate, so then would you need a few years of work in order to get it back into a good workable condition.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would tender this document, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 1D1212 will be Exhibit D217.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And I see the time, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic. Thank you. Mr. Susa, this is the end of the hearing today. You will be expected to be back at 9.00 tomorrow morning. In the meantime, you continue to be a witness and to be under oath, and that has two particular implications. The first one is that you can't discuss your testimony with anybody. Not someone at -- on the street, in the hotel. Not even your family members. And the second implication is that you can't have contact at all with any of the parties.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 8th day of October, 2014, at 9.00 a.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
